quote: It is easy to show that this edict works in contexts where there are objectively defined good solutions to problems.
content: Fable grants that the edict is "in better shape than its citation" (Orlitzky & Hirokawa 2001). On individuals, Johnson & Raab studied handball players choosing passes in fractions of a second, recognition-primed experts in a regular environment. That is where Kahneman and Klein say intuition can be trusted. The essay's context is the opposite case: "a very tough problem," Friendly AI, a problem nobody has trained intuitions for. The closest evidence on a solitary expert facing a hard problem supports the essay. In an analysis of diagnostic errors in internal medicine, premature closure, settling on the first diagnosis that fits, was the single most common cognitive failure (Graber, Franklin & Gordon 2005). Half a second of intelligence is a solitary problem, and so is the fix.

quote: If you’re an evolutionary biologist, anyone you meet can instantly solve any open problem in your field, usually by postulating group selection.
content: The amateur's group selection is Wynne-Edwards's version: traits evolve "for the good of the species." The field rejected that for good reason, and nothing in the multilevel revival restores it. Wade needed extreme artificial group selection to get his effect. Wilson & Wilson's point is that the Price equation lets any multilevel account be restated as kin selection and inclusive fitness (Wilson & Wilson 2007). If the two framings are equivalent, invoking group selection adds no explanatory power, and the question the field spent fifty years on stays open, now with better bookkeeping. The layperson at the party is not proposing Price-equation partitions. The jab stands, and The Tragedy of Group Selectionism in Book III makes the argument in full.
